newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela rejects tax write-off for black business.
newsitem.headline: Mandela rejects tax write-off for black business.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela met black business leaders on Monday and rejected their request that his government write off up to 7.5 billion rand in unpaid tax.
"Complete anarchy and chaos would be introduced if we granted your request," Mandela told delegates from the National Federation of Chambers of Commerce (Nafcoc).

Nafcoc, which says it represents more than one million members in small and medium enterprises, asked Mandela for a complete write-off of all tax, penalties and interest on unpaid tax owing from the period before April 1994 when the democratic government was voted into office.

"Our members were part and parcel of the political struggle and had to comply with the call by political organisations that taxation without representation is tyranny," Nafcoc said in a written submission to Mandela.
"We are convinced that it is grossly unfair for anybody to compel our members to pay tax owed to a government that was illegitimate and unrepresentative of all its citizens," Nafcoc said.
But Mandela, flanked by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and revenue service officials, told them: "This demand cannot be granted...the government simply can never grant that demand."
The president said he was aware of the gap between small businesses, which were largely black, and big business, which was almost exclusively white.

"We are very sensitive to the problems of small and medium-size business, and we are going out of our way to address it," he said, telling the Nafcoc delegates they should discuss repayment details with Manuel and his officials.
Manuel said a total of about 7.5 billion rand was outstanding, but about one third of this amount comprised penalties and interest that could be written off under tax amnesties.
"Our people are faced with tax debts that have reached such proportions that they are simply not able to pay," Nafcoc said.
"Thus any move to compel them to pay will unfortunately amount to ... financial catastrophe."

Mandela said he fully sympathised with their position but said: "We do not want to be accused of giving an exemption to a separate group of businessmen whereas businessmen throughout have been paying their income tax."
He said that if an exemption was granted, then a legal precedent could be set under which those who had paid taxes would demand their money back from the government.
